planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Pink Icicle camellia is valued for cold-hardy, reliable winter bloom in cold-tolerant camellia breeding lines.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Pink Icicle camellia is valued for cold-hardy, reliable winter bloom in cold-tolerant camellia breeding lines. Semi-double to peony-form flowers open a soft, cool pink with a lighter, almost frosted edge to the petals, blooming reliably through the coldest part of winter on a vigorous, upright shrub bred from cold-hardy camellia lines developed to extend the range of camellia cultivation into colder climates than the classic Gulf South and coastal camellia belt. Its combination of improved cold tolerance and dependable winter flower production has made it a popular choice for gardeners at the northern edge of camellia hardiness wanting to grow this classic Southern shrub outside its traditional warm-climate range. Mulch well to protect roots through winter, provide the dappled shade and acidic soil all camellias require, and avoid planting in a site exposed to harsh winter wind.

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Chinese stewartia needs consistent moisture and dislikes hot, dry conditions or root disturbance.

directions: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Chinese stewartia needs consistent moisture and dislikes hot, dry conditions or root disturbance. Smooth, flaking, multicolored bark in patches of gray, tan, and cinnamon provides outstanding winter interest, complemented by white, camellia-like summer flowers with prominent yellow-orange stamens and rich orange-red fall foliage color, giving this small ornamental tree four full seasons of garden interest. Related to camellias and prized among collectors for its combination of showy summer flowers, exfoliating bark, and vivid fall color on a manageable small-tree scale, it makes an outstanding specimen for a shaded woodland garden or Asian-style planting. Provide consistent moisture and protection from hot afternoon sun and drying wind, mulch well to keep roots cool, and avoid disturbing the root zone once established, since stewartias transplant and establish slowly.

directions: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Tall stewartia needs consistent moisture and dislikes hot, dry conditions or root disturbance. Among the largest-growing of the stewartias, this Japanese species develops smooth, richly colored cinnamon-red exfoliating bark considered by many collectors to be the finest of any stewartia, alongside small white summer flowers and reliable orange-red fall color, all on a taller, more substantial tree form than most of its garden-scale relatives. Its combination of eventual larger size and exceptional bark color makes it a valuable specimen tree for a spacious woodland garden where its slow but steady growth into a true small-to-medium shade tree can be accommodated over the years. Provide consistent moisture, dappled shade, and acidic, humus-rich soil, and avoid disturbing the root zone once established, since stewartias establish and transplant slowly.
